# One invocation stands the run up and finishes it

`rimsky compose run` needs no deployment to exist beforehand. It stands the
stack up, applies the manifest, drives every declared instance to terminal, and
leaves nothing listening when it returns.

## The manifest

```yaml
project: one-shot-demo
templates:
  - path: ./template-success.yml
    tag: pass
    state: deployed
  - path: ./template-failure.yml
    tag: fail
    state: deployed
instances:
  - template: pass
    name: alpha
  - template: fail
    name: beta
```

Both templates name the bundled `verifier-shape-checks` executor: one's check
passes, the other's fails.

```yaml
name: shape-checks-pass
version: "1"
message_queue_mode: backlog
nodes:
  - type: verify
    executor: verifier-shape-checks
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          checks:
            type: array
            default:
              - kind: no_nulls
                config:
                  fields: [id]
                severity: error
          rows:
            type: array
            default:
              - id: 1
```

## Run it

```bash
rimsky compose run rimsky-compose.yml
```

Nothing needs to be running first, and no endpoint needs to be configured.

## What the product does

The single invocation stands the stack up, applies the manifest, wakes both
instances, and reports each reaching terminal before it returns:

```
alpha: success (nodes=2)
beta: failure (nodes=2)
```

It exits 1 — the mixed-outcome class. The invocation waits for real outcomes
rather than for dispatch.

## Nothing to tear down

The control-API port the run allocated for itself, named in its own transcript,
refuses connections once the command returns. Nothing remains listening from the
stack the invocation stood up, so there is no teardown step — which is what
makes the invocation runnable on a machine with no provisioned rimsky
infrastructure.

The run's durable artifact directory stays on disk; see the audit-artifact
example for reading it back.
